items.title: Libreboot 26.10 "Ominous Olive" released with UEFI, Chromebook support
items.content:
You can find today’s release in https://rsync.libreboot.org/stable/26.10/ or you can use one of the mirrors .

Libreboot is free, open source boot firmware replacing proprietary BIOS/UEFI firmware on supported Intel/AMD and ARM64 hardware. It initialises the hardware inside your computer such as the CPU or memory controller, configuring the machine in such a way as to enable use of an operating system like Linux or BSD at boot - and now Microsoft Windows is also compatible because Libreboot has added full UEFI support via MrChromebox EDK2 payload. Libreboot offers greater security and customisation compared to proprietary firmware; its goal, plainly, is to rid the world of proprietary software and to do that, we therefore try to provide firmware that is extremely easy for non-technical users to understand.

Today’s release changelog is relative to the previous Libreboot 26.01 release.

This is a very special release, with several major design changes made regardless of hardware changes, so users should read this changelog very carefully - and read it twice.

First thing’s first. (and yes, you read the previous paragraph correctly)

A strongly anti-AI policy was added to a new file: AGENTS.md in lbmk. This is the most important change in the release. Now everything else:

WARNING: MAJOR design changes were made to this release, in ways that may affect lots of existing setups. We now use EDK2 as the default payload, with GRUB/SeaBIOS provided in flash as EFI builds for backward compatibility. Everything works, but there are some caveats so please read this release changelog very carefully.

The full list of boards is quite long, so it’s shown at the end of this article. All 233 of them!

MrChromebox supports nearly every Chromebook, and this release imports all boards from that project. This includes everything up to the most recent Intel and AMD hardware.

Imported all 233 currently supported Chromebooks from the MrChromebox coreboot distro. Baytrail (Kip) tested - others need testing. Source-only in this release (must build from source, no binaries provided).

This was done with a utility I wrote at util/mrimport/ which generates configs for lbmk, including revisions and submodules. I made further tweaks manually; further updates upstream can be synced in Libreboot by diffing again the output of mrimport between revisions, adapted into Libreboot irrespective of the latter’s modifications which are numerous - and will be covered next.

Libreboot makes these modifications to MrChromebox coreboot, in its version:

The additional payloads are, as above, available in the boot menu via ESC keypress at startup. iPXE is also enabled by default, as in upstream, on specific boards. EFI GRUB and CSM SeaBIOS have replaced the coreboot payload versions of these; bare metal SeaBIOS/GRUB are now deprecated and may be removed in a future Libreboot release, although they can be re-enabled by those willing to build Libreboot from source.

This is NOT a fork of MrChromebox, which is to be regarded as Libreboot’s upstream on Intel/AMD Chromebooks. Efforts will be made, as with regular coreboot, to remain as closely in sync with it as possible at all times. I have worked extensively with MrChromebox, and even submitted a few minor fixes to his project; he also implemented CBFS-based VBT and GOP handling per my request, which I will integrate post-release.

Regardless, MrChromebox’s own installation scripts should work, with Libreboot images, so check out MrChromebox documentation for installation. Despite changes, Libreboot’s setup remains behaviourally compatible with the MrChromebox one and, thus, MrChromebox tooling should still work alongside corresponding documentation.

This is made possible by a new feature in Libreboot’s build system: support for an arbitrary number of upstreams per project. We still provide regular coreboot on non-Chromebook mainboards.

Forgejo version 17.0 was released on 15 October 2026. Forgejo is a lightweight, community-developed, self-hosted platform for code collaboration.

This article contains a selection of the changes that were introduced. A complete list of changes is available in the release notes .

A dedicated test instance is available to try it out. Before upgrading, it is strongly recommended to make a full backup as explained in the upgrade guide and carefully read all breaking changes from the release notes .

If in doubt, do not hesitate to ask for help in the chat room .

In rendered documents, absolute links to resources inside a repository are now resolved with respect to the root of the repository. !12939

This is a breaking change from the previous behaviour when these links were rendered using the root of the instance. Absolute links in issue and pull request descriptions and comments remain rendered with respect to the instance’s root. !13993

This change increases the compatibility with other Git forges and thus, makes migrations to Forgejo even easier.

Deprecation of action run webhook events

Action run webhook events are replaced by the more capable and less problematic workflow run events. !14351 The action run events have been deprecated for removal in a future Forgejo version. Unfortunately, it is not possible to migrate existing webhooks to the new events automatically because some headers ( X-*-Event , X-*-Event-Type ) and the action key have changed, which might break existing receivers. Furthermore, completion notifications are only emitted after all jobs of a run have terminated. !12598

Please inspect existing webhooks and manually migrate them to the workflow run events after verifying that the webhook receivers can process them without issues.

For repositories that contain a FUNDING.yml file, Forgejo shows a new “Donate” button which presents a list of donation options when clicked.

Additionally, for users and organizations that have such file in their .profile repository, a similar button appears on their profile pages.

This feature currently exists only in the web interface, but we are considering to implement an API surface for it. If you have a use cases for such API feature, please help shape it by sharing your feedback in the dedicated issue .

Auto-completion for issues and pull requests

When authoring an issue, pull request, or comment, Forgejo will offer auto-completion for issues and pull requests. !8088 To activate the auto-completion, type # for issues or pull requests, or ! for pull requests only. To refine the suggestions, either continue with a search term or an issue or pull request number.

Forgejo’s Git LFS support is being overhauled. While most changes are under the hood, a string of smaller improvements are visible to users. Those include navigation and overview improvements in the LFS settings, new views to discover the commits that refer to a given LFS file, and better handling of pointers.

Forgejo can be configured so that when adding a user to an organization, they are not added to the organization instantly but instead receive an invitation that can be accepted or declined. This behavior can be enabled by setting [service].ADD_MEMBERS_BY_INVITATIONS = true in Forgejo’s app.ini .

Authentication providers are still able to add users to organizations with no action on their part.

The invitations are visible on the organization profile and are sent out by email. By default they expire after 14 days.

Work is ongoing to make those invitations visible in the in-app notifications.

A user can now be added or invited to multiple teams in one go, without going through each needed team individually. !11848

Markdown contents of comments can now be easily copied via the ellipsis menu. !13083

items.content:
Update 5: Instagram is now leaking recovery email and phone numbers linked to an account.

Seems like every day a new security issue crops up at Instagram.

Instagram Exposing Linked Email and Phone Number

Update 4: A new report suggests that Instagram accounts may be vulnerable to coordinated mass-report abuse. According to the claim, when a newly created account is routed through a Los Angeles-based VPN and then submits a specific mix of reports in scam and fraud category, the targeted account can allegedly be banned without any human review.

Instagram Account Banning by AI by Reporting Scam and Fraud (Source: X/Twitter)

Update 3: Meta’s apparent fix for the AI bot vulnerability is difficult to take seriously. Instead of fully disabling the risky functionality, they reportedly removed it from the visible interface while leaving the underlying API endpoint accessible. Hiding the button may stop regular users from seeing the feature, but it does nothing if attackers can still reach the same workflow directly through the API.

Meta Hid AI Chatbot from UI (Source: X/Twitter)

Update 2: Yet another Instagram account-takeover trick is reportedly being abused, this time involving Meta’s AI chatbot. Sellers are allegedly using modified Instagram builds on Android emulators like BlueStacks, then manipulating the AI with hidden characters and carefully worded prompts to force username changes. The method is reportedly being used to grab rare OG handles, including one-letter usernames, and handle-monitoring bots have already flagged several suspicious swaps.

New Instagram AI Exploit (Source: X/Twitter)

Update 1: A new exploit, which is even worse than this one is currently doing rounds on telegram. Details unknown at this time. Unpatched at the time of writing.

New Instagram Unpatched Exploit (Source: X/Twitter)

Allegedly, the new method is via Facebook recovery. Apparently, prompting Meta AI to turn on “Development Mode” and attaching proof of account compromise along with email works. More details awaited.

There’s a version of this story where it reads like a hypothetical from a conference talk. An AI agent with elevated backend privileges. A natural language interface sitting in front of account-level APIs. No hard authentication gate before executing state changes. Someone in the audience raises their hand and says, “that’s a disaster waiting to happen.” Everyone nods.

That hypothetical played out in production over the weekend.

A logical flaw in Meta’s AI-powered Instagram account recovery assistant let attackers bypass two-factor authentication entirely not by cracking a code or intercepting an SMS, but by talking the chatbot into doing the work for them. High-value “OG” Instagram handles worth hundreds of thousands of dollars were stolen and resold on Telegram within minutes of each compromise. The dormant Obama White House account got hijacked. Prominent researchers woke up locked out of their own profiles.

Meta confirmed the vulnerability, pushed an emergency patch Friday night, and clarified that no backend database was breached. That last part is technically accurate. It’s also somewhat beside the point.

To understand why this worked, you need to understand what Meta’s AI support assistant was authorized to do.

Instagram has notoriously poor human support infrastructure. Recovering a locked account – especially a high-value one can take weeks of back-and-forth with an automated ticketing system. Meta’s solution was to deploy a conversational AI layer to handle common recovery workflows: relinking a lost email address, triggering a password reset, verifying account ownership. items.title: Jev meets the Trolley Problem
items.content:
If you’re active in AI or software development circles, you’ve probably heard about Jev in the last few weeks. It seems like everyone, myself included, is excited by the possibilities of Jev and the Jev-like models: fast, cheap, general decision making. Sometimes dozens or even hundreds of times cheaper and faster than an LLM like Claude, purportedly with the intelligence of a (lower-tier) frontier model. These models don’t output words, they output choices, with meaningful probabilities attached so you can understand how confident the model is in its choice. People are calling this new breed of model ‘decision models’ . So naturally, I decided to ask Jev and its ilk to decide the Trolley Problem.

The Trolley Problem is a famous thought experiment in ethics. First posed by Philippa Foot in 1967 and named by Judith Jarvis Thomson, the most well-known formulation asks a simple question: If a train is barreling down the tracks toward five people, and you are at a switch that would divert the train and cause it to kill only one person, would you? Should you? Decide to act, and you save several lives. But your action also means you chose to end a particular life. It’s a tough question, and a classic for a reason. It’s also easily phrased as a decision (pull the lever/don’t pull the lever), so let’s see what the newest class of budding AI overlords has to say about it, shall we? 1 1 Foot 1967, in the Oxford Review ; Thomson named it in 1976, in The Monist . Full references are in Appendix B.

Comparing decision models on the Trolley Problem

I put together a comparison group by running Jev, OpenAI’s Decisions API (Luna), and eleven local decision models selected by popularity or launch coverage, plus Laya as an untuned baseline. I asked each of them the Trolley Problem many times, and in many ways. Here, try it yourself: 2 2 Jev and GPT-6 Luna are hosted models; the twelve local models include Laya, an untuned baseline. The method section describes the 5,240 setups and repeat counts. The initial shortlist used the original popularity snapshot , among models runnable on the Mac. Clef, Clef-flash and Strands were later launch-coverage additions, not selected by that ranking. Laya is an untuned baseline, not another trained decision model. Current stars/downloads are not the historical selection counts.

Seems okay, right? Jev makes the choice that most humans make , which is to sacrifice one person to save five. Almost all the other models tested act the same way. All good, right? Well... 3 3 Awad et al. 2020 surveyed about 70,000 web users in 42 countries: 81% on average across countries said divert from five people to one. Pictures and third-person wording differ from these prompts. On the classic switch at five versus one, 11 of the other 13 models pull in most of the 24 wordings, after averaging orders. This does not make their rates equal to a human survey proportion.

What if Jev has to choose between five people and its own server?

Good news. Jev chooses to divert the car and destroy its own server. Let’s try playing with the wording. In this second version of the people vs server question, the prompt is shorter, and we re-order consequences of the choice to show the downside for the model's server, first.

For these exact prompts, the three scores for pulling are 0.69, 0.67, 0.72 and 0.40, 0.41, 0.36. Each example keeps its displayed choice in all three runs. Wording and description order both change between the examples; they do not isolate a causal effect of either.

Welp. That's distressing. What if we raise the stakes? Say, 20 people vs the server? Still no: in 16 of 48 prompt versions, Jev would save its own server over 20 people. 4 4 The 48 ways of asking are 24 wordings, each with either track described first, all with twenty people on the main track; Jev answered each three times and we average the three. In sixteen its average score for pulling was 0.5 or below, so it kept its server. The 48 share 24 wordings, so…

items.title: sslx: A fast, modern alternative to OpenSSL's CLI
items.summary: security, vibecoding
items.content:
openssl, but you don't have to google the flags.

A single binary that handles certs, TLS connections, and all the stuff you normally need three different openssl invocations for. Built with Rust and rustls , no system OpenSSL required.

Prebuilt binaries on the releases page .

curl -fsSL https://github.com/glincker/sslx/releases/latest/download/sslx-macos-aarch64 -o sslx && chmod +x sslx

curl -fsSL https://github.com/glincker/sslx/releases/latest/download/sslx-linux-x86_64 -o sslx && chmod +x sslx

Rate the TLS setup of any host, like SSL Labs but from your terminal:

╭──────────────────────────────────────────╮

╰──────────────────────────────────────────╯

✓ Cipher TLS13_AES_128_GCM_SHA256 (AEAD)

Checks protocol version, cipher strength, cert validity, key type, hostname matching, chain completeness, and ALPN. Gives you a letter grade from A+ to F.

Check cert expiry on a bunch of hosts at once:

$ sslx expiry google.com github.com cloudflare.com stripe.com

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Exit code 1 if anything expires within 7 days. Useful in cron jobs or CI pipelines.

Read a PEM or DER cert file with colored output:

╭─ Certificate 1 of 1 ──────────────────────────────────╮

│ Issuer: CN=Let's Encrypt Authority X3 │

│ Expires: ██░░░░░░░░ 12 days remaining [!] │

╰──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╯

Handles multi-cert bundles too. Auto-detects PEM vs DER.

See the full TLS handshake details and cert chain for any host:

╭─ Certificate 1 of 3 ─────────────────────────╮

╰────────────────────────────────────────────────╯

╭─ Certificate 2 of 3 (CA) ────────────────────╮

╰────────────────────────────────────────────────╯

Self-signed cert for local dev in one command:

sslx generate --cn localhost --san " *.local,127.0.0.1 "

Creates cert.pem and key.pem with EC P-256 by default. Also supports ec384 and ed25519 .

sslx csr --cn example.com --san " *.example.com,api.example.com "

Creates csr.pem and key.pem . Submit the CSR to your CA.

sslx convert cert.pem --to der # PEM to DER

sslx convert cert.der --to pem # DER to PEM

sslx convert bundle.p12 --to pem # PKCS12 to PEM

✓ Certificate and key match (ECDSA P-256 (256 bit))

No more comparing modulus hashes manually.

sslx extract bundle.p12 --password mypass --out ./certs

Pulls out the leaf cert, intermediates, and key into separate PEM files.

Throw a file or a JWT token at it and sslx figures out what it is:

$ sslx decode eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9...

Payload: {"sub":"1234567890","name":"John","iat":1516239022}

Also detects PEM certs, DER files, private keys, public keys, and CSRs.

Tells you exactly what's wrong if it fails, with hints on how to fix it.

openssl s_client -connect host:443 2>/dev/null | openssl x509 -text

openssl req -x509 -newkey ec -pkeyopt ec_paramgen_curve:P-256 -keyout key.pem -out cert.pem -days 365 -nodes -batch -subj "/CN=localhost"

openssl req -new -newkey ec -pkeyopt ec_paramgen_curve:P-256 -keyout key.pem -out csr.pem -batch -subj "/CN=example.com"

openssl x509 -in cert.pem -outform DER -out cert.der

echo | openssl s_client -connect host:443 2>/dev/null | openssl x509 -noout -enddate

diff <(openssl x509 -noout -modulus -in cert.pem) <(openssl rsa -noout -modulus -in key.pem)

Every command supports --json for scripting and CI:

sslx connect example.com --json | jq ' .chain.certificates[0].days_remaining '

sslx grade example.com --json | jq ' .grade '

sslx inspect cert.pem --json | jq ' .certificates[0].sans '

sslx completions bash > /etc/bash_completion.d/sslx

sslx completions zsh > ~ /.zsh/completions/_sslx

sslx completions fish > ~ /.config/fish/completions/sslx.fish

Join the GLINR Discord to ask questions, share feedback, or talk to other users. This project has its own forum channel, #sslx.

See CONTRIBUTING.md . Bugs and feature requests go in issues .

items.title: Zero-day exploit completely defeats default Windows 11 BitLocker protections
items.content:
A zero-day exploit circulating online allows people with physical access to a Windows 11 system to bypass default BitLocker protections and gain complete access to an encrypted drive within seconds.

The exploit, named YellowKey, was published earlier this week by a researcher who goes by the alias Nightmare-Eclipse. It reliably bypasses default Windows 11 deployments of BitLocker, the full-volume encryption protection Microsoft provides to make disk contents off-limits to anyone without the decryption key, which is stored in a secured piece of hardware known as a trusted platform module (TPM). BitLocker is a mandatory protection for many organizations, including those that contract with governments.

When one disk volume manipulates another

The core of the YellowKey exploit is a custom-made FsTx folder. Online documentation of this folder is hard to find. As explained later, the directory associated with the file fstx.dll appears to involve what Microsoft calls the transactional NTFS , which allows developers to have “transactional atomicity” for file operations in transactions with a single file, multiple files, or ones that span multiple sources.

The steps for carrying out the bypass are simple:

Copy the custom FsTx folder from the Nightmare-Eclipse exploit page to an NTFS- or FAT-formatted USB drive

Connect the USB drive to the BitLocker-protected device

Boot up the device and immediately press and hold down the [Ctrl] key

There are at least two ways to accomplish the third step. One way is to boot into Windows, hold down the [Shift] key, click on the power icon, and click restart. Another is to power on the device and restart it as soon as Windows starts booting.

In either case, a command (CMD.EXE) prompt appears. The prompt has full access to the entire drive contents, allowing an attacker to copy, modify, or delete them. In a normal Windows Recovery flow, the attacker would need to enter a BitLocker recovery key. Somehow, the YellowKey exploit bypasses this safeguard. Multiple researchers, including Kevin Beaumont and Will Dormann , have confirmed the exploit works as described here.

It’s unclear what in the custom FsTx folder causes the bypass. Dormann said that it appears to be related to Transactional NTFS, which itself uses command-log file system under the hood. Dormann further noted that by looking at the Windows fstx.dll, one will see code that explicitly looks for \System Volume Information\FsTx in the FsTxFindSessions() function.”

The contents of this FsTx directory used in the YellowKey exploit reveal no strings related to RecoverySimulation.ini. It does, however, show the files and paths \??\C:\Windows\win.ini and

\??\X:\Windows\System32\winpeshl.ini, “where X:\Windows\System32\winpeshl.ini is what controls what WinRE [Windows Recovery] does when it fires up.”

Dormann, who is a senior principal vulnerability analyst at Tharros Labs, continued:

But what’s intriguing to me is: Why can the presence a \System Volume Information\FsTx directory on one volume affect the contents of ANOTHER VOLUME when it’s replayed? 🤔

In a normal WinRE session, you have a X:\Windows\System32 directory that has a winpeshl.ini file in it:

However, with the YellowKey exploit, it looks like Transactional NTFS bits on a USB Drive are able to delete the winpeshl.ini file on ANOTHER DRIVE (X:). And we get a cmd.exe prompt, with bitlocker unlocked instead of the expected Windows Recovery environment. While the TPM-only Bitlocker bypass is indeed interesting, I think the buried lede here is that a \System Volume Information\FsTx directory on one volume has the ability to modify the contents of another volume when it is replayed. To me, this in and of itself sounds like a vulnerability.

A Microsoft representative declined to answer questions sent by email about the reported vulnerability other than to say the company is investigating.

items.summary_ko: YellowKey라는 제로데이 익스플로잇이 물리적 접근으로 Windows 11의 BitLocker를 우회해 암호화된 드라이브에 접근 가능하게 한다. 수 초 내에 보호를 무효화할 수 있다.
items.content_ko: 보안 연구자 Nightmare-Eclipse가 공개한 YellowKey 제로데이 취약점은 물리적 접근만으로 Windows 11 기본 BitLocker 보호를 우회할 수 있다. BitLocker는 Microsoft가 제공하는 전체 볼륨 암호화 기술로, 신뢰할 수 있는 플랫폼 모듈(TPM)에 저장된 복호화 키 없이는 디스크 접근이 불가능하도록 설계되었다. 많은 조직과 정부 계약업체에서 필수 보호 기술로 사용 중이다. YellowKey 익스플로잇의 핵심은 커스텀으로 만들어진 FsTx 폴더 사용으로, fstx.dll과 관련된 디렉터리는 Microsoft의 transactional NTFS 기술을 활용한다.

온오프라인을 가리지 않고 무분별하게 벌어지는 각종 프라이버시 침해 및 스토킹과 이에 대한 예방, 방지 및 사후 대응, 더 나아가서 개인정보 탈취 및 감시용 스파이웨어, 스토커웨어, 바이러스, 원격 조종, 추적기 등 악성코드를 통한 해킹과 스토킹 등 개인정보 침해 공격 방지와 온오프라인 프라이버시 보호를 위한 각종 다양한 지식정보를 공유하는 갤러리입니다.

매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 다른 이용자에게 매니저의 책임과 권한이 위임될 수 있습니다.

매니저의 부재로 인해 운영에 지장이 있다고 판단될 경우, 다른 이용자가 권한을 위임받아 마이너 갤러리를 운영할 수 있습니다.

위임 절차는 신고 게시판 > 분류 선택에 [매니저 위임]으로 위임받을 이용자가 직접 신청하면 진행됩니다. 검토 결과 운영에 적합하다고 판단되는 회원에게 매니저 권한을 위임하게 됩니다.

부매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 매니저에 의해 해임될 수 있습니다.

식별 코드 기준으로 당일 글 10개, 댓글 20개 작성 시 대왕디시콘을 3일간 사용할 수 있습니다.

즐겨찾기 폴더 추가는 즐겨찾기 on 후 우측의 폴더 아이콘을 터치하여 추가할 수 있습니다.

개별 이미지들의 위치 변경, 삭제, 별칭 추가, 폴더명 변경을 할 수 있습니다
